structure.title: Act I · The dead king has an audience
structure.text: The guards see something before the prince does. Once the Ghost speaks, Hamlet has a private command concerning a public crime. The men who saw the apparition cannot confirm the story it told him.

structure.title: Acts II–III · Experiments at court
structure.text: Courtiers arrange meetings and station listeners behind walls. Hamlet hires actors to perform an experiment on his uncle's conscience. Almost everyone is collecting evidence by secretly altering the situation they want to understand.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · Other people's fathers
structure.text: The consequences of Hamlet's actions reach a second family. Laertes comes home prepared to act upon a certainty Hamlet has spent much of the play trying to obtain. The question of succession grows pressing for people outside the Danish court as well.

people.name: Hamlet and Horatio
people.text: Horatio can stand beside the prince, see the same actor or apparition, and give an independent account. In a court where friendship routinely becomes employment, that independence has an extraordinary value.

people.name: Ophelia
people.text: Father and brother both instruct her how to interpret Hamlet's attention. The court treats her knowledge of him as something it can put to use. Her own reasons for wanting an answer receive remarkably little hearing.

people.name: Claudius and Gertrude
people.role: The king and his new queen
people.text: Hamlet's uncle has married his brother's widow. Publicly they present the marriage as a settlement after bereavement. Hamlet watches his mother's conduct as intensely as his uncle's, although what he needs to know about each differs.

context.title: The danger of obeying a ghost
context.text: The audience sees the Ghost. That settles its appearance and leaves its intentions open. Hamlet himself entertains the possibility of a spirit exploiting his grief to induce a murder. His need for a second source has consequences for the staging.

notice.text: Count the audiences in the play scene.
notice.why: There is the court watching the actors, Hamlet watching Claudius, and Horatio watching at Hamlet's request. Where you look determines which drama you see.

notice.text: Listen to what a sentence becomes halfway through.
notice.why: Alone, Hamlet can start with an accusation and end up putting its author on trial. A soliloquy is sometimes the sound of an idea going wrong while he speaks.

opening: Hamlet's father is dead, his mother has married his uncle, and everyone would like him to stop making things uncomfortable. Then a ghost tells him the death was murder. Revenge sounds straightforward until Hamlet has to establish what happened, decide whom he can trust, and become someone capable of carrying it out. Meanwhile the court watches him think. Shakespeare gives him enough wit to make almost anyone look foolish and enough doubt to turn every possible action into another reason to hesitate.
